cards.title: Why "The Morning Star is the Evening Star" shocked 19th-century logicians
cards.body: If words only point to real-world objects, then stating that the Morning Star is the Evening Star should convey the exact same information as saying Venus is Venus. Yet the first statement represents an astronomical discovery. Gottlob Frege resolved this paradox in 1892 by distinguishing between an object's reference (the physical entity) and its sense (the way that entity is presented to our minds).

cards.title: The dilemma that exposed a major blind spot in utilitarian math
cards.body: Philosopher Bernard Williams asked what happens when a traveler named Jim must choose: shoot one innocent captive to save nineteen others, or refuse and watch a warlord execute all twenty. Standard utilitarianism claims Jim has an obvious moral duty to shoot. Williams countered that this ignores personal integrity—the idea that our deepest moral commitments cannot simply become pawns dictated by another person's evil project.

cards.title: Why defining "good" as anything physical always leaves an open question
cards.body: If "good" simply meant "causing pleasure," asking whether a pleasurable act is good would be as silly as asking if an unmarried man is a bachelor. In 1903, G.E. Moore pointed out that for any natural definition—like pleasure or evolutionary survival—we can still meaningfully ask: "Yes, but is it good?" Because that question always stays open, Moore argued goodness cannot be reduced to physical facts.

cards.title: How a locked room proves you can act willingly without having a choice
cards.body: In 1689, John Locke imagined a sleeping man carried into a room to converse with a dear companion. Upon waking, the man enthusiastically chooses to stay and talk, completely unaware that the door is locked from the outside. Locke noted that while the man stayed voluntarily, he lacked the freedom to leave. The thought experiment proved that voluntary action does not require having alternative physical possibilities.

cards.title: Why a young idealist drafted a contract to protect his future self from himself
cards.body: Philosopher Derek Parfit described a young socialist nobleman who inherits land and pledges to give it away to peasants. Knowing people often grow selfish with age, he signs a binding legal contract and tells his wife never to revoke it, even if his older self later demands it. Parfit used this scenario to argue that our future selves might practically function as entirely distinct people with competing moral claims.

quizzes.question: How did Gottlob Frege explain why "The Morning Star is the Evening Star" conveys new information?
options: By arguing that the two terms refer to entirely different celestial bodies
By distinguishing between an object's reference and its mode of presentation (sense)
By proving that identity statements are always mathematically uncertain
By asserting that language cannot describe physical astronomical objects
quizzes.explanation: Frege showed that two expressions can have the same physical reference (Venus) while presenting different senses (modes of presentation).

quizzes.question: What core philosophical critique did Bernard Williams make using the "Jim and the Indians" thought experiment?
options: Utilitarianism fails to account for an individual's personal integrity and moral boundaries
Utilitarian calculations always result in the death of innocent people
Human actions are entirely determined by biological instincts rather than ethics
Moral duty can only be decided through democratic voting procedures
quizzes.explanation: Williams argued utilitarianism reduces moral agency to impersonal math, ignoring a person's integrity and core life projects.

quizzes.question: What is the core premise of G.E. Moore's Open Question Argument?
options: No ethical claim can ever be debated in plain language
For any natural property like pleasure, asking whether it is genuinely good remains an open question
Morality is an illusion created purely by evolutionary competition
Pleasure and moral goodness are mathematically identical concepts
quizzes.explanation: Because one can always meaningfully ask if a natural quality (such as pleasure) is good, "good" cannot simply be defined by that quality.

quizzes.question: What did John Locke demonstrate with his thought experiment of the man in the locked room?
options: A person can act voluntarily even when alternative choices are physically impossible
Nobody can ever be held accountable for actions taken while indoors
Sleepwalking removes all moral responsibility for legal crimes
Physical imprisonment always eliminates a person's ability to reason
quizzes.explanation: The man willingly chose to stay and talk, even though the locked door prevented him from having the physical freedom to leave.

quizzes.question: In Derek Parfit's thought experiment, why does the young Russian nobleman bind his future self with a contract?
options: He fears his older self will lose his socialist ideals and revoke the gift to the peasants
He wants to prevent his wife from inheriting his family estate
He believes legal contracts expire automatically when a person turns fifty
He seeks to prove that property ownership is physically impossible
quizzes.explanation: Parfit used the scenario to explore whether a person's future self can be viewed as a distinct moral entity whose future wishes can be restricted.

misconceptions.claim: If an action produces pleasure or aids survival, it is by definition morally good.
misconceptions.explanation: G.E. Moore's Open Question Argument showed that natural qualities like pleasure are not synonymous with goodness, as asking if they are truly good remains an open debate.

misconceptions.claim: You cannot perform an action willingly unless you have the physical freedom to choose otherwise.
misconceptions.explanation: Locke's locked room thought experiment demonstrated that a person can act entirely willingly while being physically prevented from doing otherwise.
